newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan entrepreneur labours to rebuild his country.
newsitem.headline: Afghan entrepreneur labours to rebuild his country.

text.p: Zais Haidary was juggling relief projects for his Afghan aid organisation and scrambling to find blankets for a hotel he's rebuilding when word came that fighting might have broken out in the Salang Pass.
"Of course if there's really fighting in the pass it's very bad news for me and for Afghanistan," said the 45-year-old entrepreneur.

"Frankly i doubt the report is true. I hope it's not since that's how we travel to Kabul and the east. But we're used to these conditions. We've done more than 350 projects since 1989 and we worked in Kabul through the worst of the war."
Haidary emigrated from Afghanistan to the United States in 1974 and was leading the good life in San Francisco when he felt the call to do something for his native country.

"I had just puchased a new bedroom set and a mattress with a 25-year guarantee and I was lying in bed watching television and feeling very pleased with myself when a news report came on showing Afghan refugees living in tents looking miserable," he recounted.
"I felt guilty and ashamed and it was at that moment I first got the idea to try to help my fellow Afghans."
Haidary founded a relief organisation, Reconstruction and Development Association (RDA), and has been operating inside the country since 1989.

Having worked as a contractor and later as a property developer in California as well as in state government there, he had the project management skills and political savvy necessary to operate in Afghanistan's dangerous, faction-ridden environment.
RDA now employs 250 people full-time and another 700 who work on various of projects, a fact Haidary takes enormous pride in.

"When I look at at the number of people we employ and look at the difference that makes not just to their lives but to the six or seven other members of their immediate family whom they are supporting it gives me a lot of satisfaction," he said.

"Add to that the benefits of the projects themselves -- irrigation projects, school projects, whatever -- and I think we are making this country a little bit better. Of course it's not very much as compared to what needs to be done, but it's something."
Haidary prides himself on being able to work in all parts of the country, even in those controlled by ultra-conservative Taleban forces who now control about two-thirds of Afghanistan.

With a wife and two daughters living in the United States, he is relatively relaxed about Taleban's Islamic edicts banning women from the workplace and requiring them to be covered from head to foot and escorted by a male relative when they venture outside the home.

"The Taleban offer peace and security to the population in areas they control but it is security at a high price. It is like the security in a jail where your freedom is restricted. Nobody stays in jail long unless they have to," he reasoned.

"This is a temporary situation. The Taleban are Afghans and sooner or later they will behave like Afghans. A society without music or women -- what kind of life is that for people? Afghanistan has its own culture which is even older than Islam."
Haidary has two active hotel projects in Afghanistan -- one in Jalalabad and the other in Mazar-i-Sharif.
He said he soon grew tired of travelling outside Kabul, encountering destruction everywhere and never finding a decent place to sleep, eat or wash.
Two years ago he took local authorities in Jalalabad on as partners and began restoring a dilapidated hotel there. A month ago he did the same in Mazar-i-Sharif.

"The only ones who can do business in Afghanistan now are people who can take risk because business here is such a gamble. I won't make any money but i can employ local people and provide a service which my country needs," he said of his hotel ventures.

"I am keeping the hotels very simple, very basic. Just a clean place to eat and sleep where you can wash up. It is especially important to have such places for foreigners who visit Afghanistan or they want to pack their bags and leave right away."
What Zaid Haidary really longs for is a return to the pre-war Afghanistan he grew up in and left as a young man.
"I remember Kabul as a university student. It was a beautiful city. You could walk the streets at night with your girlfriend and people wore whatever they wanted," he recalled.
"Those were the good old days for me. I will not leave Afghanistan until there is peace again like there was then."
